extracted.intended_audience: writers, critics, and educated readers interested in literary criticism and composition (especially epic poets and essayists)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating 'sentiments' (thoughts, speech, and behaviour) in epic or heroic poetry, plus related advice on polite raillery and audience-sensitive treatment of faults in prose. Emphasises fit to character/subject, naturalness and sublimity, and avoiding affectation, vulgarity, or ill-timed humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience-sensitive treatment of faults
rubrics_metrics.description: You should take along with you the Distinction of Manners of the World, according to the Quality and Way of Life of the Persons concerned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat subjects (especially vices or misfortunes) in a manner proper to the sort of readers and the social quality of the persons discussed. Avoid exposing faults in a way that drags other readers into participation of the disadvantage; if a topic would disgust some readers, tailor your tone or avoid explicit detail. Remedy for offended readers is to forbear reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polite raillery: soften accusations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Rule of polite Raillery, is to speak of a Man's Faults as if you loved him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid blunt, defamatory labels for occasional faults (e.g., a man guilty now and then of intemperance should not be called a 'Drunkard'). Use mild phrasing and affectionate irony (example: Cæsar calling a railer 'a careless Fellow'). Aim your ridicule so it can be seconded in conversation rather than alienating the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tenderness when treating women's faults or misfortunes
rubrics_metrics.description: This Tenderness towards them, is much more to be preserved when you speak of Vices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing about women (particularly about fallen women), preserve delicacy and avoid indelicacy or unnecessary exposure. Do not give vices their most terrible or disgusting aspect in contexts intended for polite company (e.g., the tea-table).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentiments must conform to characters
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sentiments in an Epic Poem ... are just when they are conformable to the characters of the several Persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that what characters say and do fits their established character and status. This includes internal consistency and plausibility of belief, motive, and speech across the poem's cast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentiments must be adapted to the subject (things as well as persons)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sentiments have likewise a relation to Things as well as Persons, and are then perfect when they are such as are adapted to the Subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match the tone, scope, and manner of thought to the epic subject matter; sentiments suitable to one subject may be improper for another. Consider how lines of thought relate to the topic and the poem's thematic aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentiments must serve the intended emotional ends
rubrics_metrics.description: If ... the Poet endeavours to argue or explain, to magnify or diminish, to raise Love or Hatred, Pity or Terror, or any other Passion, we ought to consider whether the Sentiments he makes use of are proper for those Ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose thoughts and speeches that effectively produce the desired emotional response (pity, terror, admiration, etc.). Evaluate whether particular sentiments are fit instruments for the poet's rhetorical/emotional aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pursue naturalness and sublimity
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two kinds of Sentiments, the Natural and the Sublime, which are always to be pursued in an Heroic Poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a balance of believable, natural sentiments and elevated, sublime thoughts. The sublime (great, transporting ideas) is particularly prized in epic poetry; lack of sublimity may make a poem less triumphant in its genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affected or unnatural thoughts
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two kinds of Thoughts which are carefully to be avoided. The first are such as are affected and unnatural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steer clear of artificial, forced, or overly refined conceits and rhetorical puffery. The critic cites examples of later poets' 'false refinements' and lists Ovid, Lucan, and others as prone to such faults. A poet should prefer just, natural expression over theatrical artifice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mean and vulgar thoughts
rubrics_metrics.description: The second [kind of Thoughts to avoid are] such as are mean and vulgar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not admit low, grovelling, or petty sentiments into an heroic poem; these degrade the epic tone. Some classical authors (Homer in places) have such homeliness attributable to their age, but it is a blemish in epic composition generally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid burlesque or laughter-raising sentiments in epic (allow rare, well-timed relaxation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentiments which raise Laughter, can very seldom be admitted with any Decency into an Heroic Poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic poetry should rarely aim to provoke laughter; humour risks collapsing the poem's dignity. Exception: very well-timed, context-appropriate moments of mild mirth (e.g., a carefully placed comic scene in a book of diversions) may be tolerable. Avoid strings of puns or puerile pleasantry (Milton's described passage is singled out as 'exceptionable').

rubrics_metrics.name: Invented or non‑natural characters require fitting, original sentiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton's Characters, most of them, lie out of Nature, and were to be formed purely by his own Invention. It shews a greater Genius ... to have drawn his Calyban, than his Hotspur or Julius Cæsar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating characters not drawn from ordinary human observation (mythic, supernatural, or prelapsarian figures), the poet must supply apt, imaginative sentiments that suit those invented natures. Such invention demands greater judgment and care to maintain plausibility within the poem's world.
